news.title: Cat’s whiskers: Nan Goldin proves that she’s the greatest US artist since Warhol – review
news.description:
Hayward Gallery, London
The photographer finds echoes of Caravaggio and Greek myth in her erotic images, while her disturbing animal montages show that while humans can be beautiful, we are far from innocent

It’s the dirty realism of Nan Goldin’s images, her unfazed photography of the rough seams of spontaneous, dangerous lives, that enables her to create a film of such unlikely ambition as Stendhal Syndrome. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen.

She infects you with it in a ravishing work housed in what looks like a bronze yurt entered via a vaulted corridor. If this seems ostentatious, the film justifies the ceremony. A montage of sensual images teems with Goldin’s uniquely raw, immediate feel for the human presence as she photographs her friends, mostly in the nude, legs wrapped round each other, or lying in a swoon, or touching themselves, or bathing together. Here is the unfeigned, honest impact her work has had since she first put her world viscerally on camera in her early photo series The Ballad of Sexual Dependency. But there’s a difference.

A lot of strange and scary stuff happened in 1989 at Heol Fanog, a lonely farmhouse at the foot of Bannau Brycheiniog (formerly known as the Brecon Beacons). English artist Bill Rich and his pregnant Welsh partner, Liz, moved there with Bill’s teenage son to begin again, replacing the complexity of urban life with the still silence of the remote countryside. But their new start became a protracted nightmare when they experienced what seemed to be supernatural phenomena – and the Heol Fanog ghosts would keep appearing to the Rich family for another seven years.

The case – nicknamed the “Welsh Amityville” for its similarities to the US’s most famous instance of reported paranormal activity – has long haunted Danny Robins, presenter of the podcast and BBC Two TV series Uncanny, in which he investigates claims of interactions with the undead. Heol Fanog stands out because of the sheer number of eerie events, the length of time across which they took place, and the multiple witnesses: if you can explain this, what about that? Or that? Or, oh my God, THAT?

news.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
news.description:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of sexism. But one of the tragedies of Labour’s 18 long years of exile from power and the climactic defeat of organised labour in the miners’ strike was the fact that they opened the way for the wholesale reinvention of work and watershed developments that we seem to be only just waking up to.

news.title: Why I won’t leave mathematics, despite AI solving centuries-old problems | Ken Ono
news.description:
I believe human judgment remains essential


Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics?

In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned.

Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. A former vice-president of the American Mathematical Society, he is known for his work on Ramanujan and integer partitions.

These views do not necessarily reflect those of Axiom Math, the University of Virginia, the National Academies, or any other institution with which I am affiliated.

A software update is always discombobulating, but the latest one brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense (that mental image you just got of me waving my fist at the sky: spot on). Harrumph.

Days later, bored on the bus, I began answering my husband’s texts with the terrible suggested AI responses, to see if he’d notice. (We’ve been married a long time; this is how I get my kicks now.)

news.title: The Guardian view on Serbia’s new political era: a generational opportunity must not be wasted | Editorial
news.description:
Brussels must find ways to show concrete support for a new government that will genuinely share the EU’s democratic values

Following the extraordinary election that swept Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government from power, Serbia’s new political era has begun. Outside the National Assembly in Belgrade last week, large crowds celebrated as MPs from the victorious Student List movement were sworn in. Doctors, lawyers and academics put forward as candidates by the youthful protesters, who took on Mr Vučić, are now tasked with running an expectant country.

Their defining challenge will be to restore trust and democratic legitimacy in a nation that, under Mr Vučić’s bullying rule, plunged towards the bottom of Europe’s corruption rankings. Legal action has already begun against figures accused of illicitly profiting from the previous regime, while the new parliament’s elected speaker – a professor and organic farmer – called for the restoration of dignity and tolerance to its proceedings in his first address. Ensuring academic and media independence, and reforming the security services, which acted as the former president’s authoritarian enforcers on the streets, will be urgent priorities.

news.title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial
news.description:
The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. The inspection that led to the downgrading of her primary school to “inadequate” was judged to have contributed to her death. In its 2024 manifesto, Labour promised to replace one-word labels with more nuanced overviews of schools’ performance.

It is obvious now that the relationship was coercively controlling. A divorced father, he had a need to control every aspect of my life, so no makeup, no northern accent, no fatty food (I became anorexic), no scent, no staying out, no heels, no clothes he didn’t like.

I learned that he had done it all before, pursuing schoolgirls. I tried to break free multiple times, only to find that he had phoned my new partner, or read my diary so he could block my plans. This is about having control, it is not just a sexual preference.

news.title: The link between nurturing and masculinity  | Letter
news.description:
Clincal psychotherapist Gareth Strangemore-Jones responds to an article on persistent assumptions about masculinity

Sarah Blaffer Hrdy’s research offers an important challenge to one of our most persistent assumptions about masculinity: that nurturing is somehow contrary to male nature (Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so, 17 November). As a clinical psychotherapist, I find the most compelling implication is not simply that children benefit from involved fathers, but that fathers themselves may change through the experience of caring.

We often imagine psychological development as a process in which attitudes must change before behaviour follows. Yet caregiving may work in both directions. Repeated experiences of responding to another person’s vulnerability can engage and potentially strengthen the biological and psychological systems involved in emotional responsiveness, attachment and cooperation.

news.description:
This most unpredictable and evenly contested Women’s Super League campaign took another unexpected twist as Manchester City missed the chance to return to the top of the table as they suffered a second successive defeat, by virtue of a terrific performance from a Tottenham side who moved within three points of the European places.

The shock result came just 24 hours after City’s title rivals Chelsea had dropped points at Liverpool. It was the first time City had failed to win a home league match during Andrée Jeglertz’s 16 months in charge, let alone lose.

Continue reading...

news.title: NFL roundup: Chiefs, Lions and Bills march on; Metcalf ejected for eye poke in Steelers loss
news.description:
• Bears also continue strong start to season

  • Ravens go down to sixth-straight loss

Greg Rousseau had two sacks, including his team-leading 10th of the season, and Buffalo’s defense bailed out the Bills’ sputtering Josh Allen-led offense in a win over the injury-depleted division rival Miami Dolphins (1-9). Allen was limited to a four-yard touchdown pass to DJ Moore with two interceptions in an outing during which Buffalo settled for three field goals on five drives inside Miami’s 20. James Cook scored on a one-yard run for Buffalo (9-1) and had 89 yards rushing to become the NFL’s second player to score a TD and top 75 yards rushing in nine consecutive outings. Miami has lost four straight and are off to their worst start to a season since going 0-13 to open 2007.

Continue reading...

news.title: Video of ICE detaining father and daughter while boarding flight sparks protests in Seattle
news.description:
Footage of Saturday incident, filmed by fellow passengers, quickly went viral on social media as mayor calls tactics ‘un-American’

Protesters marched through the Seattle-Tacoma international airport on Sunday after widely shared footage captured masked immigration agents detaining a father and daughter on an airport jet bridge as they boarded their Alaska Airlines flight.

Video of the incident on Saturday – filmed by fellow passengers – quickly went viral on social media, sparking condemnation from lawmakers, including Washington Democratic governor Bob Ferguson and Seattle mayor Katie Wilson.

Continue reading...

news.title: Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations
news.description:
As nationalist, Eurosceptic parties surge in four of the bloc’s biggest member states, the coming year’s polls could test its resilience like never before

In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain, Lionel Jospin was prime minister of France, and Gerhard Schröder had just been elected chancellor of Germany. The EU had 15 member states and pro-European, centre-left parties were in power – either alone or in coalitions – in all but two of them.

Brisk economic growth was lifting living standards. Eastward enlargement was under way. In Washington, Bill Clinton was pursuing the same brand of “third way” centrism as a middle path between free-market capitalism and traditional socialism. The EU felt like it had the tide of history behind it.

Continue reading...

news.title: Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages
news.description:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes

Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.

Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.

Continue reading...

news.title: UK taxpayers held more than £1tn in offshore tax havens, latest HMRC data shows
news.description:
Figures show recent 10% rise in total held in financial centres such as Jersey and Panama, raising fears over cost to public purse

The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purse.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data, obtained by the TaxWatch thinktank through freedom of information requests, shows between 2022 and 2024 the value of balances held offshore in tax havens increased by 10%. These were the latest available figures.

Continue reading...

news.title: US army to blow up bomb-making chemicals despite safety concerns
news.description:
Army invokes emergency provisions in Iowa to avoid court order despite worries about health and environment risks

The US army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder.

“To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” government lawyers told the eight US circuit court of appeals in a filing late on Saturday. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”

Continue reading...

news.title: Cloned number plate victims in England and Wales to get new reporting tool
news.description:
Police launch initiative after steep rise in criminals using method to evade detection and avoid paying penalties

Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32 driving fines she received this summer after her car’s number plate was cloned.

Yarwood’s black Volkswagen Golf did not move from outside her London home while she was on holiday in Canada, but a similar vehicle with a fraudulent copy of her registration racked up penalty notices totalling £2,560 across five London boroughs.

Continue reading...

news.title: ‘Intimidating’ vigilantes posing as far-right security on the rise, UK experts say
news.description:
Volunteers in black uniforms and body armour increasingly seen with figures such as Tommy Robinson

There is a worrying rise in “reckless and intimidating” vigilantes posing as security guards around far-right figures, security experts have said.

In recent months, uniformed figures wearing all black and body armour have been seen in the entourages of far-right figures including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, who goes by the name Tommy Robinson, and Paul Golding, the leader of the far-right political party Britain First.

Continue reading...

news.title: Bank of England directors illegally profited from post-abolition enslavement in Cuba
news.description:
New research finds that the British-led Cobre Mining Company helped industrialise Manchester via copper deposits and enslaved African people

• Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds

British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research.

Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian Chris Evans has found.

Continue reading...

news.title: CEO of funding agency for UK science and research criticised by union over cuts
news.description:
Exclusive: Prospect’s Mike Clancy tells Ian Chapman at UKRI that union has ‘lost confidence’ in his leadership

A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and research, citing concerns about plans for major cuts.

The letter from Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, to Ian Chapman, the chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), is the latest development in a row over changes in funding for projects and research facilities.

Continue reading...

news.title: US releases files on suspected Bigfoot sightings in Montana and Oregon
news.description:
Forest Service releases files months after residents in rural Ontario reported encounters with massive figures

Bigfoot has quietly appeared again.

Well, not Sasquatch directly, but new files about the cryptid.

“The stride of the tracks did not change with slope.”

“The tracks at both sites were not to the ‘bottom’ of the mud.

“The small toes lack a definite ‘pad’ at the tips as would be expected.”

Continue reading...

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed doubles down on ‘TrumpCare’ health plan, urging president to ‘get it done’
news.description:
Democratic senator-elect reiterates suggestion to rename Medicare for All after Trump if president allows bill to pass

Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage.

“If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.”

Continue reading...

news.title: Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says
news.description:
John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips

Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.

Continue reading...

news.title: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
news.description:
Warning about putting ‘genie back in the bottle’ comes as UN conference fails to agree on regulation instrument

The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to put the “genie back in the bottle” as the development of autonomous weapons appears to outpace efforts to regulate them.

The stark warning came as more than 120 member states of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded a week-long conference in Geneva.

Continue reading...

news.title: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
news.description:
Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long

British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.

Continue reading...

news.title: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
news.description:
District court in the Hague finds Chinese carmaker infringed on intellectual property of Jaguar Land Rover

Chinese carmaker BYD has been banned from selling its “Defender clone” vehicle in the EU by a court in the Netherlands, after Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) brought a case saying it infringed intellectual property rights.

JLR launched legal action over the seven-seater Ti7 SUV earlier this year after BYD announced on its website that it was taking orders from UK customers for the vehicle. Earlier this month, bailiffs acting for JLR were reported to have seized digital records from BYD’s offices.

Continue reading...

news.title: Black Friday deals for liquid Brazilian butt lifts criticised over safety fears
news.description:
Experts say BBLs and other cosmetic procedures can be risky and seasonal offers at clinics in England could make people rush decisions

Clinics in England are promoting seasonal deals – including for Black Friday – on liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), despite concerns about the risks of the procedure.

The government is consulting on limiting liquid BBLs, vampire facials and deep chemical peels in England to qualified healthcare professionals. The proposals follow the death of Alice Webb, a 33-year-old mother of five, after a botched liquid BBL in a Gloucester salon in 2024. Her family have called for laws against “cosmetic cowboys” to be introduced before more people die.

Continue reading...

news.title: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?
news.description:
The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that

Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success.

Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic.

Continue reading...

news.title: Grammy snubs and a Stevie Wonder vs Lauryn Hill Showdown | The Close Up Culture Swap
news.description:
The Grammy nominations are here, and Carys and Lanre are celebrating by swapping their favourite Album of the Year winners. Plus: the snubs we have beef with.

Raye, Olivia Dean and Olivia Rodrigo, we hope you clean up at the awards in February. But this week, we’re going back to the classics.

Stevie Wonder’s Songs in the Key of Life or The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill: does either deserve to be framed? What would your rating be? Basement, bottom, mid, top or Frame It? Tell us in the comments

Continue reading...

news.title: SNL’s skit Sister captures the quiet agony of caregiving for women: ‘I’ve never felt seen like that’
news.description:
The viral satirization of the caregiving burden left to women and daughters hit home for many viewers

The Saturday Night Live sketch, titled Sister quickly went viral this week for its satirization of the burden that women and daughters face to take care of aging family members. In the parody commercial, comedian John Mulaney touts the benefit of “Sister”, who he describes as “a live-in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister”.

“Now I don’t have to worry about dad getting the care and attention he needs because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life, and the stuff I like to do,” Mulaney says, as the sister, played by cast member Jane Wickline, gives their father’s medication to him.

The sketch, which amassed over seven million views on YouTube in less than a week since it aired, has received thousands of responses and comments about its accuracy.

“This is one of the MOST wicked and spot on SNL sketches ever written,” wrote one commenter on YouTube. Another posted: “As a hospice nurse this definitely tracks. I deal 90% of the time with adult daughters, and if there is no daughter, it is the daughter in law.”

“This is so real it almost gave me a stroke from rage,” added another viewer.

Continue reading...

news.title: ‘I’m opening the cage of a monster’: Taxi Driver scriptwriter Paul Schrader on unleashing AI at 80
news.description:
Director and Scorsese collaborator is using AI in films and sees its takeover as inevitable, not just in cinema

Paul Schrader was sipping white wine in a Greenwich Village trattoria when he said how he felt about using AI to make films: “I am opening the cage of a monster and I don’t have a leash.”

The 80-year-old film-maker behind Taxi Driver, Raging Bull and American Gigolo, is embracing the technology as he enters the final act of a prolific career in which he has collaborated with Martin Scorsese, Robert De Niro, Sigourney Weaver and Richard Gere.

news.title: ‘In the office, there was a sharp intake of breath’: why has the BBC decided to celebrate Christmas earlier than ever?
news.description:
Festive specials are being released on the iPlayer as much as a month before the big day. Is this a dire flouting of tradition – or a welcome modernisation? TV insiders analyse the change

Traditionally, around this time of year, people remark that Christmas feels as though it’s coming earlier than ever. In the BBC’s case, it actually is.

Mortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Christmas Fishing, The Repair Shop at Christmas and other festive BBC specials will be available to watch on iPlayer from 27 November, up to a month before these shows debut on the television itself. This means you can watch Mary Berry avidly talk about the joy of eating mince pies, followed by a Christmas-themed murder in the Caribbean in Death in Paradise, well before the tree is up (unless, of course, you put up your tree earlier than ever, too).

Continue reading...

news.title: Bill’s Included review – Rob Brydon’s new character is as glorious as Gavin & Stacey’s Uncle Bryn
news.description:
The comic is sublime as a middle-aged landlord attempting to befriend student tenants. It’s very sweet – but the storylines and supporting characters are flimsy to say the least

Bill Beam (Rob Brydon) is a chump, a sap, a bejumpered limpet clinging to the peripheries of his own existence. “I’m being left behind,” he tells best friend Drew (Kevin Eldon) who, having heard this – and that, and the other – a thousand times before, stifles a well-earned yawn. Bill’s wife has left him for the gardener (“No hard feelings!”) and lo, this ever-dimming bulb of cable-knit neediness must find a solution to both his newfound “cashflow crisis” and deepening existential haplessness. What to do?

Enter, stage left, a fire at the local student halls and, with it, an answer to the plonker’s prayers: Bill will rent out his spare bedrooms to four undergraduates. Yes! This will provide him with the requisite dosh, a much-needed sense of purpose and a fresh audience for his piping-hot takes on Jeremy Beadle, the big Asda and the fact that his phone number is “one of only nine UK landlines to conclude with the digits 1, 2, 3, 4.” Go tell it on the mountain! But bring a sad trombone while you’re at it. Because, astonishingly, Bill’s young tenants aren’t hugely keen on the idea of a divorced sixtysomething in pink trousers attempting to shoehorn himself into their lives. Not least when said shoehornery entails impromptu balloon-animal demonstrations and announcements of the “Don’t think of me as a landlord. I’m a landfriend” variety.

Continue reading...

news.title: Interpol and Bloc Party review – two of 00s indie’s most revered acts go toe-to-toe
news.description:
Utilita Arena Cardiff
Kele Okereke has a tough challenge selling Bloc Party’s trite latest album – a far cry from Interpol’s ‘masterpiece’ eighth record, performed here to darkly hypnotic effect

Try as one might to resist comparison, the balance of this particular yin and yang has been shifting for some time. Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era.

Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners.

news.title: ‘I do a really good version of AC/DC’s Highway to Hell, which throws people’: Sharleen Spiteri’s honest playlist
news.description:
The Texas singer was fascinated by Elvis Costello as a kid and admires Nancy Sinatra’s sass and strength, but which of her own songs changed her life?

The first song I fell in love with
My mum gave me an old Dansette record player and a pile of albums. I must have been eight or 10, with my younger sister Corinne, getting butterflies to These Boots Are Made for Walkin’ by Nancy Sinatra. Years later, I read that she was told to sing it with a much more provocative attitude. You can hear the sass and the strength. Maybe that’s where my whole “don’t fuck with me” thing came from.

The song I do at karaoke
Give me any Marvin Gaye song, like You’re All I Need to Get By, and I’m all over it, but I’d normally pull someone up to duet with me.

Continue reading...

news.title: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness
news.description:
M&S Bank Arena, Liverpool
Just a few years since playing little dive bars, the Irish rockers have confidently scaled up to huge rooms like this – and are now one of the key interpreters of modern malaise

A mere seven years since their debut, Dogrel, Fontaines DC have enjoyed a virtually seamless passage from Dublin dive bars to arenas, with stadiums to follow next year. Each step has been taken seemingly effortlessly in their stride and this latest outing is no exception. Bathed in shimmering blue light, the band are well into hymnal opener Six Shot Morning before we even see sight of singer Grian Chatten. He wanders on while singing, an entrance worthy of Frank Sinatra.

Chatten has previously seemed to distrust showbiz, but if anything the singer seems far more comfortable on the bigger stage than he ever did on smaller ones. With his Korn T-shirt, unfeasibly baggy trousers and tiny tattoo reading “deadly” in capitals, he leaps around, raises his arms to whip up the crowd and points the microphone towards them to sing key lines. Similarly, music this intense, dark, elegiac and even bleak – which speaks to the void at the heart of much modern life – is hardly typical arena fare but works brilliantly by taking on a more anthemic, celebratory aspect. It’s certainly weirdly thrilling hearing Chatten’s lines such as “We’re all depressed, running on a wheel” or “I don’t feel anything in the modern world” – or a song as plainly dark as Jackie Down the Line – become enormous, arena-uniting sing-songs.

Continue reading...

news.title: Nothing compares to her: Sinéad O’Connor’s 20 best songs – ranked!
news.description:
The Irish singer-songwriter would have turned 60 in early December. To mark the occasion, we revisit the best of a catalogue that’s far more than a certain Prince cover

This suitably uncompromising opener to the lengthy Faith and Courage offers a collage of radio static, Indian-inspired beats, dub bassline and whispered vocals. More importantly, it’s fantastic: you might call it trip-hop were Sinéad O’Connor’s vocal not so intense as to negate any potential for relaxation on the part of the listener.

news.title: The footballer-turned-BookTuber who made an obscure Tolstoy novella a belated bestseller
news.description:
Once named the best player in Brazil, Gustavo Scarpa’s literature obsession has inspired thousands to become bookworms

Julián Scatolaro noticed something odd was occurring when several people came into his bookshop over the space of a few days, all asking for Leo Tolstoy’s novella The Death of Ivan Ilyich.

The 35-year-old, who owns a bookshop in the small Argentine city of Chajarí, 311 miles from Buenos Aires, said the sudden interest in a book written in 1886 was surprising enough. But this was particularly strange because when his customers ask for works by the Russian writer, they usually want War and Peace. In a video he posted about the mystery, he called it the “Tolstoy enigma”.

news.title: ‘Harsh to be under her thumb’: Pitchfork’s Ryan Schreiber on selling to Condé Nast and Anna Wintour
news.description:
He shocked the industry when he ‘sold out’ to corporate media in 2015. For the first time since leaving, he opens up about his new life as an out gay man and why he quit

On the early November day that I met Pitchfork founder Ryan Schreiber in New York City, the website he created is all that anyone on my timeline can talk about, again. Today, it’s thanks to a freshly dug-up tweet from Jon Ossoff, the newly re-elected Georgia senator, who sincerely wrote in 2012: “Looking forward to your writeup of the new @imaginedragons album.”

It’s an all-timer, up there with Phoebe Bridgers saying that she thinks about the site’s review of Jet’s second album (a video of a monkey pissing in its own mouth) once a day, and Halsey wishing that the Pitchfork office, which is on the site of the 9/11 attacks in New York, would “collapse already”. The joke in Ossoff’s case is that Pitchfork would not be caught dead praising the purveyors of stomp clap radio rock; a 2021 review characterized the band’s music as “emotions fired out of a T-shirt cannon”.

Continue reading...

news.title: Light in the dark: 20 long books for short winter days
news.description:
Turn off your phone, get cosy and commit to some of literature’s biggest and best novels. From Don DeLillo’s Underworld to The Luminaries by Eleanor Catton, these epic reads are worth taking your time over

Life starts all over again when it gets crisp in the fall,” wrote F Scott Fitzgerald in The Great Gatsby, and after the beach reads of summer, now feels like the time to settle down to more ambitious projects. Not slim works like Gatsby, but the bigger beasts you have been circling for some time. A book to wrap yourself up in as autumn becomes winter.

The year I spent reading The Lord of the Rings when I was eight made me want to be a writer. The novel’s scope and the sheer amount of time I lugged it around with me combined, so that whatever I was doing, part of me was always thinking about it. This is what long books, in particular, can do.

Continue reading...

news.title: Promise Me, America by Joe Biden review – former president defends his decisions
news.description:
New memoir tells of policy feats and battles with Trump but struggles to take responsibility for re-election debacle

Inevitably, readers of Joe Biden’s new memoir will flick forward to find what he says about the events that ended his presidency: increasing pressure about his age and capacity that finally led him to stand aside and anoint Kamala Harris, too late, ushering fascism back to the White House. Alas, Biden thinks he was just fine to keep on serving and the whole thing was a stitch-up by a panicked party.

Of his catastrophic debate in June 2024, when the then 81-year-old president blinked, stuttered and gaped under the lights, Biden writes: “I knew the debate had gone badly. But I knew that debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent presidents. Especially their first ones. I left the stage thinking I would be debating Trump once more before the election was over. I was wrong. This wasn’t just the first debate, it was my last one.” He raises Barack Obama’s poor performance in his first debate with Mitt Romney in 2012, when Biden was VP. Caught cold, Obama prepared for the next one and cruised to re-election.

Continue reading...

news.title: The Guide #270: Grand Theft Auto VI is everywhere – but is it really the cultural event of the decade?
news.description:
In this week’s newsletter: It could be the biggest entertainment release ever, but its reach reveals the limit of shared cultural experience

An estimated cost of $1bn. A development period of 13 years. A production team of 5,000 people. A game map the size of Manchester. An estimated 24m copies sold through pre-orders and launch day alone, generating $2.36bn. Thousands upon thousands of days of leave booked and sick days taken to play the thing, costing the US economy an estimated $1bn (yep, another billion figure) in lost productivity. The scale of Grand Theft Auto VI – and the tidal wave of facts and figures surrounding its making and economic impact – truly boggles the mind.

Even if you, like me, are unlikely to ever sit down and play the thing, you will struggle to escape its influence. Footage both sinister and benign – from graphic shooting sprees to mellow clips of its protagonists strolling, hand in hand, down the beach – will follow you around Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok. Whatever your preferred publication, left or right, high- or lowbrow, it will have proffered its own take on the game, whether it’s to bemoan its godless influence on adolescent men or to laud its unlikely celebration of stable (if criminally inclined) relationships. It even receives extended segments on BBC News at 10 – much to the annoyance of veteran political reporters.

Continue reading...

news.title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI
news.description:
Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’

Described as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting.

While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida. GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments.

news.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
news.description:
With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre

  • Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?

In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it.

For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building.

Continue reading...

news.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
news.description:
PC; Forward Instinct
This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living

For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag.

Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed underpants off the clothesline just to make the long drive through the night worth it. I was reminded of Shameless (the US version) as much as Steinbeck.

Performed in the venue where Noye’s Fludde premiered and based on the same text, this festive new work shines with exuberant young performers, distinctive singalongs, lustrous designs and the spirit of mucking in

When Benjamin Britten wrote Noye’s Fludde, he essentially invented community opera. Bringing professionals together with enthusiastic local amateurs, everyone mucking in to play, sing and make sets and costumes, isn’t only great fun; done right, it fosters a love of music-making that can last a lifetime. Such projects, the composer declared with his best socialist hat on, created works that were “useful to the living”.

For decades, Britten contemplated a nativity opera, which somehow never transpired. Now, Errollyn Wallen, Master of the King’s Music, has filled the gap. A Christmas Miracle, co-produced by Mahogany Opera and Britten Pears Arts, sets texts from the same Chester mystery plays that inspired Noye’s Fludde, and premiered in the Orford church that Britten chose in 1958.

news.title: Roll up, roll up! Marc Chagall’s Circus is the most mesmerising big top you’ve ever seen – review
news.description:

He spent over 60 years painting clowns, ringmasters and acrobats – and the results transport you to a dazzling magical world

At the opening of The Circus, a self-portrait of Marc Chagall is placed next to a lithograph of a clown. The portrait is small and sketched simply in a blue crayon, as if Chagall had quickly dashed it out to pacify an inquisitive fan. In contrast, the clown is rich in colour and texture, with a heavily detailed backdrop of musicians, spectators and performers. But there is something uncanny about this pairing, created more than 40 years apart. They both wear small, brimmed hats with hair springing out from underneath, and their facial expressions are somewhat inscrutable.

It is the perfect introduction to an exhibition that explores Chagall’s lifelong fascination with the circus, both as a subject and as a symbolic motif. In placing Chagall and the clown side by side, we understand this immediately – the clown is both a clown and a metaphor for the artist. In his 1967 art book Cirque, Chagall writes: “This clown – he is he and I.”

I cannot say I’ve ever been a Robbie Williams fan. When I went to see Better Man, the 2024 biopic in which Williams is played by a CGI chimp, I was tagging along with my wife. To be honest, I was sceptical about the ape but tried to meet the film with an open mind. I wasn’t looking for anything in particular but what I found was something that seemed to explain my life.

I was born two months premature in Winnipeg, Canada, in 1961, with severe hearing loss in both ears that wasn’t diagnosed until I was seven. In 1969 we moved to Woking in Surrey; my father left and my mother descended into alcoholism. I was a misfit in my family, with no support for my deafness, and at school the bullying – from kids and teachers – was something awful. In my desperate isolation, I turned to reading: book reading, lip-reading, and reading the room. Forget TV, forget music – the Beano and Beezer were my survival manuals: the Numskulls taught me how my brain worked with broken ears.

news.title: Cassette, London WC2: ‘One of the greatest dishes I’ve eaten all year’ – restaurant review | Grace Dent on restaurants
news.description:
A discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the deadly bloody serious

I booked my lunch table at Cassette, a new French restaurant in Covent Garden, central London, while watching a viral video of a blasé Parisian couple, mid-riot, sipping wine and smoking Gauloises near the Arc de Triomphe. Yes, fiery flames of mass anarchy, but also, yes, finishing one’s glass is important, too. The Brits keep opening Parisian-style restaurants as a quiet admission that these people are really bloody cool, and this new one from Mark Gurney and Matt Bushnell, the pair behind Peckham’s Levan (also very cool, incidentally), serves the likes of a coq au vin jaune pie with a chicken leg saluting from its crust, and panisse with chopped mussels and green tomato. There’s also pork chop with sauce Talleyrand, Maldon oysters with beurre blanc, and a cocktail called Jet Fuel that combines Get 27, the green mint liqueur that gives every Parisian a starry-eyed memory of their parents’ dinner parties, with calvados and coffee liqueur.

Cassette is a discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the actually deadly bloody serious. Yes, dress up fancy, if you wish, but you can also slide in here in jeans and knitwear for a casual midweek vol-au-vent. No one will judge you. Service will at first come at you brasserie-style – casual, no stress – but can very quickly turn nerdy, obsessive and wallowing in ingredients, provenance and technique. If you want to geek out over bleu d’Auvergne or the consistency of the mascarpone cream, the staff will indulge you. The wine list starts at a kindly £29 a bottle, but soon climbs up into nosebleed territory via grower champagnes from the likes of Jérôme Prévost, a 2014 Jura savagnin, a detour to the volcanic Italian island of Pantelleria and a £350 Valentini trebbiano. In other words, Cassette is a clandestine foodie paradise.

The loos are nightclubby, tiled and, frankly, a bit down at heel, and the decor is pretty functional, clean and tidy, but the trump card right now is chef Essa Fakhry. In kitchen terms, Fakhry is Dublin-reared, having run the stoves at 777, a riotous contemporary Mexican and tequila joint, before going on to open Note in 2021, a wine bar that soon turned up on every “go there bloody quick” list and then slid into the Michelin Guide. After that, he put in an appearance at Planque, everyone’s favourite wine fiend’s paradise in Haggerston, east London. Now he is here in Covent Garden, lavishing all of that pedigree on quiche, creme brulee and a Saint-Marcellin cheese course – yes, indeed, the food of 1970s hostess trolleys. I’ll say this quietly, to avoid a rumpus and so that you can book yourself a table quickly: I think he’s one of the best chefs in London right now.

We popped in for just a few plates and ended up ordering much of the menu out of sheer curiosity. First, raw beef croustade with comté – tiny buttons of tartare in a micro case, if you will – with a creamy cheese sauce. Infinitely inhalable.

news.title: ‘The spirit of a borderless Europe steams from the pots and pans of Vienna’
news.description:
There’s more to the Austrian capital’s cuisine than schnitzel – its dishes come from all over the world

The Viennese love to eat. That isn’t solely a sign of joie de vivre. Sometimes it’s just hunger. The city has a long history of decline. Entire empires have crumbled here, or simply dissolved. Emperors took a final sigh and slipped under the table, ministers burst while tucking into their dessert, poets quietly starved to death or choked on their own self-importance. Vienna’s cuisine has outlasted them all: a little bit too heavy, a bit too greasy, and always covered in breadcrumbs or sprinkles.

Consider the schnitzel, for example. The Wiener Schnitzel is a legend, supposedly a dish of world-class stature: golden-yellow and wavy, spilling over the plate, with a delicate wedge of lemon daintily nestled beside it (in some of the more upmarket establishments, it even comes wrapped in a little linen pouch). There are few dishes that are so passionately raved about while being so fervently disparaged. The schnitzel has to be pounded until paper-thin, the breadcrumb coating must be light and airy, the accompanying potato salad prepared with a marinade of beef stock, vinegar, oil and finely chopped onions – without (without!) mayonnaise. Anything else is an affront. In Vienna you can get heated debates with strangers about all sorts of ideological nonsense. But the quality of a schnitzel is not up for discussion. The Viennese take food seriously, but without coming across as particularly serious. If you’ve nothing to laugh about at the dinner table, you’ve nothing to laugh about in life.

news.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
news.description:
Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine

When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it?

Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill?

news.title: Why I love Madrid in winter: ‘Locals get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats’
news.description:
The streets and squares of the Spanish capital come alive with Madrileños shopping, drinking and dining outdoors, warmed by lap blankets and patio heaters

Live in Madrid long enough and you hear the same weather-related proverbs again and again. One old saying goes that the seasons in the Spanish capital break down to “nine months of winter and three months of hell”. And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle.

Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. Many local people get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats, and one of my seasonal highlights is spotting couples or whole families engaged in furious arguments while wearing reindeer antlers or giant turkeys on their heads.

news.title: Why I love Stockholm in winter: ‘A return to slowing down, cosying up and revering every glimmer of light’
news.description:
Swedes adore the festive season, embracing the shorter days with fairy lights, yuletide feasts and fun in the snow

I’ll let you in on a secret: I often tell people that summer is the best time to visit Stockholm. Clouds drift across impossibly blue skies, we skip around midsummer maypoles singing folk songs and cruise the waterways, bobbing and weaving through the archipelago’s 30,000-plus islands.

That’s mostly because I want to keep December in Stockholm to myself. Soft white snow dusts buildings of ochre and burnt sienna like icing on a cake. Festive candles light up pavements leading to cosy cafes, where the earthy, buttery smell of seasonal saffron buns (lussekatter) replaces cinnamon buns for fika, our revered tradition of coffee and cake.

news.title: ‘The place becomes a jewellery box of glittering lights’: readers’ favourite winter city breaks in Europe
news.description:
Ice-skating, illuminated medieval buildings and seasonal treats feature in your picks of atmospheric winter cities

• Tell us about a winter weekend break – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher

In December, Antwerp is transformed into a jewellery box of glittering lights. Christmas markets throng the historic squares, and the illuminated facades of the gothic and Renaissance buildings create a magical atmosphere. At Groenplaats, we watched ice-skaters circle the statue of Rubens, while at Handschoenmarkt we listened to carols courtesy of the Singing Christmas Tree. There’s plenty to do during the daytime, too: we admired the art nouveau architecture in Zurenborg and paid homage to Bruegel’s Dull Gret at Museum Mayer van den Bergh. The famous brown cafes make the perfect place for a cosy nightcap.

He made a comeback in 2020, and his long-awaited final fight is on 11 December against Anthony Joshua. He appears with his wife, Paris, and seven children in the docuseries At Home With the Furys. A documentary charting his life, Fury, is out on Netflix on 27 November.

news.title: Readers reply: when does a reasonable train route become unreasonable?
news.description:

• This week’s question: is there any way in which ‘manifesting’ can achieve the desired effect?

I recently made a return trip to Edinburgh from London on which both legs of the journey were either significantly delayed or cancelled. At Waverley station, a message over the public address system told us we could travel by any “reasonable” route, but what does that mean? What counts as reasonable and what doesn’t? And who decides? Grant, by email

Send new questions to nq@theguardian.com.

When a journey is between stations that have one or more common routeing points, the permitted journey takes the route of shortest distance or any route no more than 3 miles longer, whether or not they pass through the common routeing point. Also permitted are journeys that use direct trains to and from the common routeing point.

news.title: The life, death and improbable rebirth of LA’s most beloved diner
news.description:
For decades, it served pancakes, hash browns and steaks to hungry Angelenos. Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back

Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad.

For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler.

news.title: Consent under scrutiny: where does youth end and adulthood begin?
news.description:

The fact that the age of sexual consent in Britain is set at 16 is thanks to a chimney sweep’s daughter from Marylebone, London, called Eliza Armstrong – not that she had any say in the matter.

In June 1885, Armstrong had just turned 13 when she was sold for sex by her alcoholic mother for the sum of £5. She believed she was going to work as a gentleman’s maid; instead, the child was taken to a brothel, where she was examined to prove she was a virgin and drugged with chloroform to await the gentleman who had “purchased” her virginity.

news.title: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth
news.description:
For three hours, Nathan Fielder opts not to quiz convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes on the details of her deception. Instead, he looks into her eyes and asks if she’s for real. Is that why his film has been so successful?

• This article does not contain major spoilers

Sometimes, people who have lied lie about whether or not they’ve lied. They even, on occasion, fail to tell the truth despite having sworn to do so – in court, for instance, or staring deeply into the eyes of someone who is sitting right there.

Is that a shock? Probably not. We all engage in versions of such behaviour every day. We understand that the current climate of mutually clueless echo chambers helps claptrap gain traction. But we can still recognise the difference between little white lies and big red flags. We know that the moment anyone starts using the phrase “my truth” it’s time to cancel the wedding.

news.title: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare
news.description:
Co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia, which is exporting climate pain

The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multiculturalism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.

The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work.

news.description:

Peter Fluck, who has died aged 85, was, with his fellow artist Roger Law, half of the Fluck & Law partnership that revived satire on TV with Spitting Image, the ITV puppet sketch show lampooning celebrities, politicians and the royal family.

Two decades after the BBC’s That Was the Week That Was spoofed the British establishment and, in particular, the last days of Harold Macmillan’s Conservative government at the time of the John Profumo affair, Spitting Image, from 1984 to 1996, mined another period of Tory rule rich in distinctive characters, exaggerating elements of their personalities.

news.title: ‘He’s open and affable – I avoid being recognised like the plague’: Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon on celebrity, friendship and their trip to the Arctic circle
news.description:
The northern lights, fine food, Melvyn Bragg impersonations – The Trip has landed in Scandinavia. We take in the sights with its stars, as they ruminate on ageing, activism and the best car to take a nap in

Morning in Valldal, and in the pale September light, the Juvet Landskapshotell stands quite still amid mountains, pines and yellowing birch. In the hotel dining room, Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon are taking breakfast; coffee and muesli and compote spread out before them as they settle into a discussion of the playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen, and their enduring infatuations with much younger women. “When Ibsen was 60, he fell in love with a teenager called Emilie,” Brydon says. “Can you imagine doing that?” Coogan swallows his muesli: “I can imagine it …”

The conversation shifts, taking in the persecuted genius of Galileo, a short exhortation on the subject of Palestine, and how the aurora borealis has just been spotted in the skies above Great Yarmouth. After a time, Brydon falls into an extended impersonation of Melvyn Bragg presenting In Our Time. “Can you expand on that?” he barks at Coogan. “Expand … Expand … Expand.” The edges of Coogan’s mouth begin to flicker.

news.title: Cop31 draft climate text dissected: what it says and what it means
news.description:
Fiona Harvey reads between the lines of the draft document that will end up outlining decisions and resolutions from the 31st climate summit

  • Cop31 live – latest updates

The final text is one of the most important documents that will come out of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey. What emerges in the latest draft here is that it will not be a new treaty, but a series of decisions and resolutions. These decisions have legal force in the context of the Paris agreement, so this is a powerful document. But it is also a document that can be accepted only with the consensus of all parties, therefore much of the language is cautious and some is ambiguous or open to interpretation, to the frustration of countries who want to move faster.

I. Global progress and context
1. Strongly reaffirms commitment to multilateralism and resolves to remain united in the pursuit of efforts to implement the Convention and achieve the purpose and long-term goals of the Paris Agreement; 2. Recalls that the Paris Agreement will be implemented to reflect equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in the light of different national circumstances; 3. Acknowledges that the Paris Agreement is working and that the global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development is irreversible, and that significant collective progress towards the Paris Agreement temperature goal has been made, from an expected global temperature increase of more than 4°C according to some projections prior to the adoption of the Agreement to an increase of around 2.6°C based on the full implementation of national climate plans; 4. Emphasizes the importance of promoting the economic and social benefits and opportunities of action on climate change, recognizing the significant drop in the cost of mature renewable energy and zero- and low-emission technologies, and the role of the energy transition in strengthening energy security, affordability and availability;

news.title: Cat’s whiskers: Nan Goldin proves that she’s the greatest US artist since Warhol – review
news.description:
Hayward Gallery, London
The photographer finds echoes of Caravaggio and Greek myth in her erotic images, while her disturbing animal montages show that while humans can be beautiful, we are far from innocent

It’s the dirty realism of Nan Goldin’s images, her unfazed photography of the rough seams of spontaneous, dangerous lives, that enables her to create a film of such unlikely ambition as Stendhal Syndrome. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen.

She infects you with it in a ravishing work housed in what looks like a bronze yurt entered via a vaulted corridor. If this seems ostentatious, the film justifies the ceremony. A montage of sensual images teems with Goldin’s uniquely raw, immediate feel for the human presence as she photographs her friends, mostly in the nude, legs wrapped round each other, or lying in a swoon, or touching themselves, or bathing together. Here is the unfeigned, honest impact her work has had since she first put her world viscerally on camera in her early photo series The Ballad of Sexual Dependency. But there’s a difference.

news.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
news.description:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of sexism. But one of the tragedies of Labour’s 18 long years of exile from power and the climactic defeat of organised labour in the miners’ strike was the fact that they opened the way for the wholesale reinvention of work and watershed developments that we seem to be only just waking up to.

news.title: Why I won’t leave mathematics, despite AI solving centuries-old problems | Ken Ono
news.description:
I believe human judgment remains essential


Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics?

In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned.

Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. A former vice-president of the American Mathematical Society, he is known for his work on Ramanujan and integer partitions.

These views do not necessarily reflect those of Axiom Math, the University of Virginia, the National Academies, or any other institution with which I am affiliated.

Outside the National Assembly in Belgrade last week, large crowds celebrated as MPs from the victorious Student List movement were sworn in. Doctors, lawyers and academics put forward as candidates by the youthful protesters, who took on Mr Vučić, are now tasked with running an expectant country.

Their defining challenge will be to restore trust and democratic legitimacy in a nation that, under Mr Vučić’s bullying rule, plunged towards the bottom of Europe’s corruption rankings. Legal action has already begun against figures accused of illicitly profiting from the previous regime, while the new parliament’s elected speaker – a professor and organic farmer – called for the restoration of dignity and tolerance to its proceedings in his first address. Ensuring academic and media independence, and reforming the security services, which acted as the former president’s authoritarian enforcers on the streets, will be urgent priorities.

news.title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial

The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. The inspection that led to the downgrading of her primary school to “inadequate” was judged to have contributed to her death. In its 2024 manifesto, Labour promised to replace one-word labels with more nuanced overviews of schools’ performance.

Sarah Blaffer Hrdy’s research offers an important challenge to one of our most persistent assumptions about masculinity: that nurturing is somehow contrary to male nature (Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so, 17 November). As a clinical psychotherapist, I find the most compelling implication is not simply that children benefit from involved fathers, but that fathers themselves may change through the experience of caring.

We often imagine psychological development as a process in which attitudes must change before behaviour follows. Yet caregiving may work in both directions. Repeated experiences of responding to another person’s vulnerability can engage and potentially strengthen the biological and psychological systems involved in emotional responsiveness, attachment and cooperation.
